opus-5.5.text:
I think the most distinctive thing effective altruism brought to this conversation, early on, was a willingness to take the possibility seriously before it was socially comfortable to do so. A lot of the people who started thinking hard about transformative AI in the 2010s came at it from an EA frame: if you're trying to figure out where you can do the most good, you have to ask which developments might reshape the world most, even if they seem speculative or weird. That habit of following an argument to its conclusion, rather than dismissing it because it sounds like science fiction, was really valuable.

The second contribution is a quantitative mindset. EA pushes you to put rough numbers on things: how likely is this, how big would the impact be, how tractable is it to work on. When I worked on forecasting when we might get transformative AI, the goal wasn't to get a precise answer. It was to make our assumptions explicit enough that people could argue about the specific inputs instead of talking past each other on vibes. I think that's helped move the field from "is this even real?" to "what are the actual cruxes?"

Third, there's the scope sensitivity piece, caring about the long-run future and about very large numbers of beings, including potentially digital minds. That makes you take seriously tail risks that a more conventional cost-benefit analysis might round to zero.

That said, I'd be honest that the EA lens has blind spots. It can be a bit insular, and it has sometimes been more focused on dramatic catastrophe scenarios than on the messier, gradual disruption that's actually unfolding now: labor market effects, concentration of power, institutions struggling to keep up. I think the most useful thing now is for those EA-originated ideas to blend with expertise from economists, policymakers, security people, and folks inside the labs who see the technology day to day. The early framing helped people notice the problem; solving it requires a much broader coalition.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that effective altruism's contribution is less about any specific technical insight and more about a posture toward the problem.

The first piece is just taking expected value seriously over long horizons. A lot of people, when they first hear that AI might be transformative, either dismiss it as science fiction or treat it as too speculative to act on. The EA frame says: if there's even a meaningful probability that we're building systems more capable than humans within a few decades, the stakes are enormous, and you should allocate attention proportionally to that, not proportionally to how comfortable or mainstream the topic feels. That's how I ended up working on this at all. I didn't come in with a strong prior that AI was going to be the biggest thing. I came in asking what the most important problems were and following the argument where it led.

The second piece is a willingness to actually try to forecast. When I wrote the biological anchors report at Open Philanthropy, the goal wasn't to be confident. It was to put explicit numbers and assumptions on the table so people could argue with them. EA culture rewards that kind of legible reasoning. You say what you believe, you say why, you say what would change your mind. That's been valuable because the alternative in most of the world is vibes. People either feel that AGI is near or feel that it's far, and there's no way to make progress on the disagreement.

The third thing, and I think this is underrated, is that EA gave people permission and funding to work on this when it was genuinely fringe. Alignment research, governance work, forecasting, a lot of that was supported by EA-aligned donors years before frontier labs or governments cared. That created a bench of people who had thought hard about these questions by the time the rest of the world started paying attention.

Now, I'd also be honest about the limitations. EA can be too insular. The community sometimes mistakes consensus within a small group for actual evidence. There's been a tendency to focus on fairly abstract misalignment scenarios while underweighting more mundane disruptions, like labor displacement or concentration of power, that are arguably more legible and more likely in the near term. And I think the movement has had to reckon with the fact that some of the people and institutions it helped build have ended up in positions where their incentives aren't obviously aligned with the mission anymore.

So my overall view is that EA contributed a serious, quantitative, long-horizon way of thinking about AI that the world badly needed. But at this point the problem is bigger than any one community, and the most useful thing EA can do is keep its intellectual honesty while being much more open to people who don't share its full worldview.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most useful things effective altruism contributes is the habit of asking, “How big could this be, who could be affected, and what can we actually do to make things go better?” With AI, it’s easy to focus on the next product release or the effects on a particular industry. Those matter, but we should also be thinking about changes that could affect society as a whole, including people who don’t have much influence over how the technology is developed.

Another contribution is taking uncertainty seriously without treating it as a reason to do nothing. You don’t have to be confident about when very powerful AI will arrive to think that preparing for it could be valuable. You can ask which actions would help across a range of scenarios, and what evidence would change your priorities.

And I wouldn’t say effective altruism has all the answers here. You need technical expertise, policy expertise, and the experience of people affected by disruption. What it offers is a starting question: given limited time and resources, where can we do the most good?

sol-6.1.text:
I think one thing effective altruism contributes is a habit of asking, “How big could this be, who could be affected, and what can we do now that would actually help?” With AI, it’s easy to focus on the next product release or the jobs that might change over the next couple of years. Those are important questions, but we should also be considering the possibility of much more fundamental changes, including changes that affect people around the world and future generations.

And then there’s an emphasis on making uncertainty explicit. We don’t know how quickly AI will advance or exactly what the consequences will be. But we still have to make decisions. So I’d want to compare different scenarios, ask which interventions seem useful across them, and be willing to update as we learn more.

I don’t think effective altruism gives us a definitive answer about AI. Its contribution is more a set of questions and habits: take large potential consequences seriously, look for neglected problems, and try to connect your concern to actions that could make a difference.
